title: Settings in a support inbox
excerpt: Put promised hours, routing, shared replies, and the mailbox connection on the first settings screen. Personal snippets and theme stay in their own group, away from the customer-facing voice.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen, a building with a few rooms that matter and many that do not.
caption: The corridor leads to a few rooms, not every room at once. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should support settings lead with?
faqs.answer: The hours you promise, how a new conversation gets an owner, the shared replies, the signature customers see, and whether the mailbox is receiving. Labels should describe what the customer or the agent will experience. A tour of apps and themes can sit lower.

faqs.question: How should saved replies be edited?
faqs.answer: Shared replies are published by a lead, with a preview that fills tokens using a sample customer, including the empty case. Personal snippets stay with their owner. A new agent should not be able to rewrite the company voice on the first afternoon.

faqs.question: Where should a dead mailbox be reported?
faqs.answer: On the connection row of the frequent shelf, not only inside a notification toggle. Agent alerts and the customer auto-reply are different promises and need different controls. A green notifications switch next to a dead mailbox will hide the real failure.

markdown:
Keep support inbox settings ux as a cabinet, not a second product. Group what an agent or a lead changes often: the replies they reuse, the hours customers are promised, and who receives a conversation. Bury the rest.

The W3C's WCAG overview frames quality as perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A setting is finished when its label says what the customer or the agent will experience, the control can be used without a codebook, and the same noun appears in the queue and in the cabinet.

## The frequent shelf

The first settings screen should hold the decisions that change today's queue.

- Hours you promise to answer, and the time zone those hours use.
- How a new conversation gets an owner: round-robin, a named queue, or leave it for the lead.
- Saved replies the whole team shares, with the names agents already use.
- The signature and the from-address the customer sees.
- The mailbox connection, and whether it is currently receiving.

Theme, keyboard trivia, and a marketplace of apps can sit lower. They are not why a founder opened settings after two customers got the wrong voice. Lead with the promise and the voice. Lead with nothing else.

Labels are outcomes. "Hours customers are promised," not "SLA configuration." "Who receives a new email," not "Routing logic." A new lead should be able to read the cabinet without a walkthrough. If they need a walkthrough, the labels are still internal.

Split "for me" from "for everyone." An agent's personal snippets and notification noise are theirs. The shared signature, the hours, and the mailbox are the company's. Mixing them on one page is how a personal experiment becomes the voice of the brand. Two groups, two headings, similar visual weight only if they are equally dangerous. They are not. Company settings sit higher.

## Hours, routing, and the sentence on the queue

Hours are a setting with a public consequence. If you promise a reply within one business day, the queue's clocks should use that definition, and the cabinet should show the same sentence the queue shows. One field. If the queue says "due in 2 hours" and the cabinet says "best effort," you have two products. Delete one.

Write the exception for holidays in the same group as the hours, not in a different app. "Closed 25 December. The clock pauses." Show a preview of what a ticket opened on that morning will display. A preview of a real sentence beats a cron expression. If you need the expression, put it behind the sentence, for the person who must debug it, not in place of the sentence.

Routing belongs beside hours because both decide who feels the wait. Each rule needs an example. "Mail to help@ goes to the shared queue. Mail to billing@ goes to the lead." If a rule can match nothing, say what happens. "If no one is on shift, it stays unassigned and visible to leads." Unassigned and invisible is how mail goes missing. The cabinet should make invisibility hard to choose, and impossible to choose by accident.

Assignment limits, such as a cap per agent, should say the overflow in text. "After 15 open conversations, new mail skips Sam and stays in the queue." Show Sam's current count if you can, so the setting is not abstract. Caps without a visible overflow become a mysterious empty queue for one person and a flood for everyone else.

## Voice: snippets, signatures, and the from-line

Saved replies are settings the customer will read. Put the frequent ones on the shelf, each with a name, the channel it is for, and a preview with tokens filled by a sample customer. "Hi Mina, order 4412 shipped." If a token can be empty, show the empty preview in the cabinet so the hole is obvious before a shift, not during one.

Say who may edit the shared set. A new agent adding a snippet called "final FINAL" to the company list is a permissions problem you should solve here, with a label, not with a scolding later. Personal snippets can be edited by the owner and used by the owner. Shared snippets are published by a lead. Draft and published, as with any other customer-facing sentence.

The signature and the from-name are the brand at the bottom of every reply. Show them as the customer will see them, including the legal line if you must have one. Keep it short enough that it does not bury the answer. The cabinet can warn when the signature is longer than the sample reply. That warning is more useful than a rich-text playground.

Changing the from-address is dangerous. Customer replies may still go to the old address, or may fail, depending on your mail. Say which, before the save. "Replies to old messages will still arrive at help@." Or "They will not. You need a forward." Give the lead the sentence to paste to the company. You are changing an address, not a preference.

## Notifications for agents, not a second inbox

Agents need a setting for what interrupts them. A sound for a new conversation assigned to them. A mail when they are mentioned. No sound for every message in a shared queue, unless they opted into that queue. Default to the quieter choice. A noisy default gets muted at the operating system, and then the mentions get muted too.

Separate customer-facing automation from agent alerts. An auto-reply that says "we got your email" is a promise, and it belongs with the voice settings, with the exact text and the hours when it sends. It should not send at 3 am if you do not read mail at 3 am, unless the text admits the clock. "We read mail on business days. Yours arrived outside those hours." Write that in the cabinet, preview it, and let a lead turn it off without turning off agent mentions.

Do not hide a failed mailbox inside notification settings. If mail is not arriving, the frequent shelf should say so on the connection row. A green "notifications on" next to a dead mailbox is a trap. The connection status is the setting that matters. The chime is not.

## Tags, queues, and the words agents already use

Tags are a setting because they become the language of search and routing. Keep the list short enough to fit in the composer's menu without a scrollbar full of near-duplicates. "Refund," "shipping," and "billing" are enough to start. "Refund maybe" and "refunds" will both get used, and then neither filter works. Edit tags in the cabinet, show how many open conversations wear each one, and let a lead merge two tags without throwing the conversations into untagged limbo. Say the merge in a sentence before it happens. "22 open conversations tagged refunds will be tagged refund."

Queues are tags with owners. A billing queue is a setting: the address that feeds it, the people who see it, and whether everyone else can see that it exists. Agents should not have a personal taxonomy that the lead cannot see, or the cabinet and the floor drift apart. If someone needs a private label, call it private, and do not let routing rules depend on it. A rule that only one person understands is not a setting. It is a favor the queue will not survive.

Read the tag list out loud once a month. Delete the ones no conversation has worn in that month, or archive them so old threads still display the word. A settings screen full of abandoned tags is how a new agent tags nothing, because choosing feels like guessing. The cabinet should make the right word obvious.

## Review the cabinet on a quiet afternoon

Change a shared reply and confirm an agent sees the published text, not the draft. Change hours and confirm a test conversation shows the same due sentence. Turn a mailbox off in a sandbox and confirm the shelf says mail will not arrive. Invite a new agent and confirm they cannot edit the company signature.

If a frequent change took a tour to find, move it up. If a dangerous change was a small toggle with no consequence written beside it, write the consequence and move it away from the daily controls. The cabinet is done when a lead can predict what customers and agents will experience after the save.

Critique is a different room. The object is a screen and the comments on it, not a customer waiting on a reply. [The first screen of a design critique tool](/blog/the-first-screen-of-a-design-critique-tool) applies the same rule there: show the next useful object, and one action, instead of a tour of the collaboration suite.

Hanabi designs this cabinet in Figma beside the queue it changes, then builds it in Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The hours, the published reply, and the mailbox status are data, which Prisma and PostgreSQL hold well. Tailwind keeps the shelf plain. Motion, if any, confirms a save. It does not walk a lead through a setup story.

When settings have turned into a second help desk, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). You want the pattern where the controls are fewer than the features, and each one shows its consequence. Bring the five settings your lead actually touches. That is the shelf.
